newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - Jan 9.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - Jan 9.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Following the High Court's Wik decision on native title, Queensland Natural Resources Minister Howard Hobbs said yesterday the State Government had suspended the issue and renewal of most mining leases and land dealing and development of leasehold propert would be frozen indefinitely. Page 1.

In Ernst & Young's 1996 International Technology in Banking survey, it is predicted that banking transactions at branches will drop from 46 per cent in 1995 to 30 per cent in 1998 and phone banking will grow from one per cent in 1995 to nine per cent in 1998. The figures follow the argument of banks that the increase in phone banking and use of facilities such as EFTPOS will make branch networks less significant by the end of the century. Page 2.

The Federal Opposition's competition spokesman Mark Latham yesterday revealed Labor Party plans to establish a network to monitor petrol prices around Australia, hence placing pressure on the Howard Government to ensure it keeps its promise of lower petrol prices. The network hopes to monitor movements in retail petrol prices in 80 towns and regional centres. Page 2.

Leaders from the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission, land councils and legal services have invited Prime Minister John Howard and Federal Opposition Leader Kim Beazley, State Premiers and mining and pastoral representatives to a Wik "summit" in Cairns on January 22 and 23. Page 4.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Queensland Natural Resources Minister Howard Hobbs yesterday called on graziers holding pastoral leases that cover 72 per cent of the State to stop all improvements to their properties or risk being in breach of the law. Hobbs' call has increased pressure on the Federal Government to clarify the native title laws following the High Court Wik judgement. Page 1.

At the North American International Motor Show in Detroit, United States, Ford Motor Company chief executive officer Alex Trotman said the company may be forced to stop its Falcon manufacturing operations in Australia if the Federal Government gos ahead with tentative plans to cut car industry tariffs. Page 1.

Following the revelation that yachtsman Raphael Dinelli, rescued by the RAAF in December, would not contribute to rescue costs despite earning about A$50,000 from media contracts, Federal Sport Minister Warwick Smith has written to his French counterpart Guy Drut calling on French authorities to ensure round-the-world yacht races are sailed in safer waters. Page 1.

As jockeys claimed yesterday to be considering forming a trade union linked to the powerful Australian Workers' Union in an effort to secure higher minimum riding fees, National Racehorse Owners' Association president Nick Columb said yesterday his organisation and the Australian Trainers' Association are planning to black-ban jockeys who threaten to strike and replace them with apprentice and renegade riders. Page 1.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

In an effort to rescue British yachtsman Tony Bullimore, who, if alive, has survived three days trapped in his capsized yacht in the freezing Southern Ocean, the Australian Navy is considering using a merchant oil tanker to come alongside Bullimore's yacht and use its giant crane to lift the craft out of the water. Page 1.

After spending 20 hours clinging to the submerged hull of his yacht, Frenchman Raphael Dinelli revealed yesterday his yacht sank just ten minutes after he reached an RAAF liferaft. He was then rescued by yachtsman Peter Goss, who yesterday docked into Hobart as Dinelli was given a medical check-up. Page 1.

Ford Motor Company chairman Alex Trotman yesterday warned the Howard Government that any moves to cut local car import tariffs to five per cent by 2004 would see the company's large-scale assembly operations in Australia threatened. Page 1.

New South Wales Board of Studies figures of the 1996 Higher School Certificate results show new selective high schools are draining the top achievers from comprehensive schools and markedly lowering the academic performances of non-selective schools acros the State. Page 1.
THE AGE

Parliament House Completion Authority chairman Bill Baxter suggested yesterday Victorian taxpayers would face a bill of between A$1 million and A$2 million for the scrapped Parliament House project, with the termination of consultants' contracts on December 24. The project was stalled by independent MP Russell Savage last month. Page A1.

The New York Post has reported that Michael Jackson is preparing to become an Australian citizen. The paper, whose report could be as accurate as the last Elvis sighting, reported Jackson hoped to become Australian to protect his assets. Page A1.

French yachtsman Raphael Dinelli almost drowned in the Southern Ocean and suffered frostbite and hypothermia before being rescued last month while competing in the Vendee Globe solo round-the-world race. Dinelli thanked Australian rescue authorities, who sent him a liferaft that he reached just 10 minutes before his yacht sank. Page A1.

Victorian Opposition health spokesman John Thwaites claimed yesterday the Royal Melbourne Hospital was treating fewer patients classed as urgent than it was a year ago, saying this was evidence that patients with conditions once considered urgent are nw being classed as semi-urgent (category two) on waiting lists. Page A1.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
